claims.text: Silicon can be introduced into a boride-based component by powder-metallurgy processing.
The silicon addition should be minor and maintained within a controlled concentration range.
Silicon in the boride material will produce a silicon-rich protective layer during exposure to molten aluminum.
The protective interfacial layer will be continuous and consist of a silicide or an Al-Si-enriched phase.
Silicon in the alloy reacts with molten aluminum to form a stable silicide layer.
The silicide layer inhibits aluminum penetration into the underlying boride structure.
Inhibiting aluminum penetration reduces corrosion of the underlying boride structure.
Silicon-doped boride will have a significantly lower molten-aluminum corrosion rate than undoped boride under identical exposure conditions.
Silicon-doped boride will degrade more slowly than undoped boride.
Silicon-doped boride will retain better microstructural integrity than undoped boride.
The protective effect is expected to remain effective at approximately 660 degrees Celsius during typical hot-dip aluminum-plating immersion durations.
Silicon concentrations outside an optimal range may cause secondary-phase formation or degradation of other material properties.
Changes in temperature or exposure time may negate the protective effect.
Minor silicon additions have enhanced oxidation or corrosion resistance in related high-temperature systems.
The effective silicon concentration range for boride components in molten aluminum is not yet established.
The magnitude of the expected corrosion-resistance improvement is not yet established.
